title: Edit by priority
summary: Protect task fulfilment, focus, organisation and development before spending limited review time on sentence-level accuracy and surface conventions.

sections.title: Fix the answer before polishing the language
content: A perfectly punctuated response can still fail if it does not answer the task. Editing therefore begins with meaning at the whole-response level, not with the first spelling mistake a learner notices. Ask first: have I completed every part of the prompt, maintained one controlling focus and given the reader a route through the response?

Use a four-pass ladder. Pass 1 checks task and focus. Pass 2 checks order and paragraph jobs. Pass 3 checks whether important claims have specific evidence and explanation. Pass 4 checks sentence control, grammar, spelling and punctuation. A later pass cannot compensate for a failure in an earlier one.

sections.title: Pass 1: compare the draft with the task contract
content: Turn the prompt into a short checklist of non-negotiable requirements. For a task asking what was learned at school, how it was applied elsewhere and what resulted, the draft must identify the learning, show a genuine transfer beyond school and explain the result or insight. Interesting material that does not meet one of these needs is secondary.

Write a one-sentence focus statement and test every major paragraph against it. If the draft describes a classroom method for half its length but never shows its use at home, add the missing application before improving vocabulary. If it answers a different question well, it still needs a content revision.

sections.title: Pass 2: reverse-outline the organisation
content: Label each paragraph by its job in five or six words: establish the problem, explain the school learning, show the application, report the result, or reflect on the lesson. Read only those labels. Repeated jobs reveal duplication; a missing job reveals a gap; a confusing sequence becomes visible without line-editing every sentence.

Order ideas according to what the reader must understand next. In a transfer response, a clear route is often problem, relevant school learning, application, observed result and reflection. This is not a compulsory template. The test is whether each paragraph prepares for the next and advances the chosen focus.

sections.title: Pass 3: repair evidence and explanation
content: Underline the central claims, then locate the specific action, observation or example that supports each one. Replace an empty claim such as ‘the experiment was successful’ with the measured observation and its limit. Add explanation where the reader otherwise has to infer why the evidence matters.

Delete or compress material that has no job. A vivid description of classroom wall colours may be accurate, but it distracts if the response is about transferring fair-testing skills to a home problem. Editing is not always adding; removal creates space for relevant development.

sections.title: Pass 4: improve sentences and conventions
content: Only after the response works as an answer should you check sentence boundaries, agreement, reference, verb forms, spelling, capitals and punctuation. Read once for one error family at a time. A focused pass catches more than changing whatever happens to look awkward.

Do not introduce a new factual claim while polishing a sentence. Preserve the evidence boundaries established in earlier passes. Correcting ‘seedling were’ to ‘seedlings were’ improves agreement; changing ‘four seedlings remained firmer’ to ‘every plant grew perfectly’ damages accuracy even if the sentence sounds confident.

sections.title: Name the level of the problem
content: Classify each needed revision as task, focus, organisation, development, sentence control or convention. Then repair the highest-level problem first. Moving a paragraph may remove a repeated transition; deleting an irrelevant sentence may remove two spelling errors automatically. Early structural decisions often make later surface edits unnecessary.

When review time is limited, protect the response's meaning and route before polishing every line. Leave a visible priority mark beside any unresolved lower-level issue, but never mistake a clean surface for a complete answer.

sections.title: Apply the editing ladder
content: Edit an original response about transferring fair-testing skills from science class to a home herb-growing problem. Decide which revision has the highest priority, repair the response's focus and order, remove irrelevant material, separate higher-order changes from surface corrections and choose the strongest final version. Complete all six decisions before viewing feedback.
